scenes.head: Revenue and cost forecasts
scenes.sub: Forecast each revenue line from what really drives it, spread a project’s years over calendar years, and build costs that behave as costs do: some with sales, some fixed and rising with inflation, some arriving in steps. Then read the forecast for what it says about the business.

segs.say: Revenue and cost forecasts. Forecast each revenue line from what really drives it, spread a project’s years over calendar years, and build costs that behave as costs do: some with sales, some fixed and rising with inflation, some arriving in steps. Then read the forecast for what it says about the business.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Choose a forecasting method for each revenue line (growth on a sound base, price times volume, a project schedule) and justify it.
Convert a project’s own years into the model’s calendar years.
Forecast variable, fixed and step costs from their drivers, including fixed costs that rise with inflation.
Build the income statement down to EBITDA, and calculate the contribution of each new activity.
Evaluate a forecast against the normalised history and explain what drives its margins year by year.

scenes.head: Ana now has a clean history and a normalised 2027 EBITDA of $73,587.

segs.say: Ana now has a clean history and a normalised 2027 EBITDA of $73,587. Coastline’s credit officer has seen enough start-up plans to know where they go wrong: revenue that grows smoothly forever, and costs that somehow do not. Ana’s forecast has to show where each dollar of revenue comes from, and costs that rise when the business grows and do not fall when it does not.

scenes.head: There is no single right way to forecast revenue.

segs.say: There is no single right way to forecast revenue. Each line is forecast from the driver that best explains it, and different lines in the same business usually need different methods. Four are common.
Growth on a base. Last year’s revenue grown by an assumed rate. Simple and transparent, and right for a line whose business is stable, provided the base is a full, normal year.
Price times volume. Units sold multiplied by the price per unit: workshops × participants × fee, cans × net price. It separates what the business sells from what it charges, so each can be tested.
Capacity. What the business can serve at most (seats × hours × turns, kitchen hours × covers) times a utilisation rate. Useful for cafés, hotels and factories, and a ceiling on any other method.
Market and share. The size of the market times the share the business expects to win. Common for new products; a check on optimism, since a forecast that implies an implausible market share is wrong.

scenes.head: Lantern’s six revenue lines use three of these.

segs.say: Lantern’s six revenue lines use three of these. The cafés, the online shop and catering are established, so they grow on their bases: the cafés from their twelve-month figure of $283,200 (not the ten-month $236,000), online and catering from 2027’s actuals. Training is forecast as price times volume, because Ana plans the number of workshops and sets the fee. The second kitchen and Cold Brew are new: their revenue comes from the project forecasts F05 used to decide on them, Cold Brew as cans times the net price per can.
Lantern’s revenue forecast, 2028–2032 (dollars)

scenes.head: The second kitchen opens on 1 April 2028, and F05 forecast it in project years that run from April to March: $150,000 of revenue in its first year…

segs.say: The second kitchen opens on 1 April 2028, and F05 forecast it in project years that run from April to March: $150,000 of revenue in its first year, $185,000 in its second, and so on. The model’s years run January to December. Calendarising converts one to the other: each calendar year takes the months of each project year that fall inside it.

scenes.head: January to March 2029 belong to the kitchen’s first project year; April to December to its second.

segs.say: January to March 2029 belong to the kitchen’s first project year; April to December to its second. 2028 takes only nine months of the first year, $112,500, with nothing before it. The kitchen’s fixed costs ($40,000 a year) and rent ($30,000) are calendarised the same way, so 2028 carries $30,000 and $22,500 of them. Cold Brew is simpler: Ana counts its launch year as calendar 2028, so its project years and the model’s years coincide.

scenes.head: A cost forecast is right when each cost moves with what really drives it.

segs.say: A cost forecast is right when each cost moves with what really drives it. Three kinds of behaviour cover most of Lantern’s costs.

Variable costs move in proportion to a revenue line: café goods at 31% of café sales, online goods at 48%, Cold Brew at $0.74 a can, cost of services at 39.6% of catering and training revenue, the kitchen’s ingredients and event staff at 42% of its sales, and event wages at 35.1% of catering revenue. Each share is measured against its own line, so the total cost of sales follows the mix.

Fixed costs do not change with sales in the short run, but they do change over time. Lantern’s fixed wages (the cafés’ staff on a twelve-month basis, the shop and office, and Ana’s salary) were $179,800 in 2027; Ana assumes pay rises of 3% a year, so they are $185,194 in 2028 and $208,437 by 2032. The café leases ($48,000) and the first kitchen’s rent ($14,400) are fixed by contract.

Step costs are fixed until the business reaches a limit, then jump. A second kitchen is the clearest example: Lantern’s catering could not grow past what one kitchen can produce, so growth required a new block of fixed costs (rent, a supervisor, utilities) at once. A forecast that grows sales past a capacity limit without the step in costs is too optimistic.

scenes.head: A few costs are forecast as a share of total revenue because they have many small drivers: card and platform fees, shipping, utilities and sundries…

segs.say: A few costs are forecast as a share of total revenue because they have many small drivers: card and platform fees, shipping, utilities and sundries together, at 9.1% of revenue, and advertising at 2%. This percent-of-sales shortcut, from F05, is fine for small, mixed costs. It is wrong for fixed costs: rent does not rise because sales do, and forecasting it as a share of sales makes the margin look stable when it would really improve with growth (or worsen in a downturn).

chapters.title: Nominal forecasts, and keeping inflation consistent

scenes.head: Lantern’s model is in nominal dollars: the dollars that will actually be paid and received in each year, including price rises.

segs.say: Lantern’s model is in nominal dollars: the dollars that will actually be paid and received in each year, including price rises. Its growth rates therefore include inflation. Ana’s 4% a year for the cafés is meant to cover menu prices rising with costs, a little under 3%, and slightly more trade. Its fixed costs rise with inflation too: wages by 3% a year. The café leases are the exception, because their payments are fixed by contract for five years, so they stay at $48,000 a year.

scenes.head: The rule is consistency.

segs.say: The rule is consistency. A model that grows revenue at nominal rates must grow its costs at nominal rates as well, or the margin will widen year after year for no reason except inflation. The opposite error is as common: costs grown with inflation and revenue held flat at today’s prices, which squeezes the margin just as artificially. F04’s lesson on real and nominal returns made the same point about rates; in a forecast it applies line by line. If a model is built in real terms (today’s prices) for a good reason, every line, and the discount rate used to value it later, must be real too.

scenes.head: Growth forecasts should be checked against what the business can physically do.

segs.say: Growth forecasts should be checked against what the business can physically do. Lantern’s two cafés sold $141,600 each on a twelve-month basis in 2027. The forecast has them selling $168,169 each by 2032, 18.8% more. Is that possible with the same seats, opening hours and staff? Roughly a fifth more sales could come from higher prices, longer hours or quicker service, but if the cafés were already full at peak times in 2027, part of it may need another barista or longer hours, both of which cost money. A capacity check does not need precise numbers: it asks whether the forecast implies something the business cannot do without spending more than the model shows.

scenes.head: The same check applies to the online shop (can Lantern pack and ship 48% more orders by 2032 with the people it has?) and to catering.

segs.say: The same check applies to the online shop (can Lantern pack and ship 48% more orders by 2032 with the people it has?) and to catering. The second kitchen is itself a capacity decision: F05 justified it by the extra catering and wholesale bakery sales it makes possible, and the model gives those sales their own line rather than stretching the first kitchen’s.

scenes.head: Every input in the forecast should carry three things beside it: its source (“F05 project forecast”, “2027 accounts”, “Ana’s estimate”), the reason…

segs.say: Every input in the forecast should carry three things beside it: its source (“F05 project forecast”, “2027 accounts”, “Ana’s estimate”), the reason for it in a few words, and, in a model several people use, who owns it and when it was last reviewed. Lantern’s inputs block lists each growth rate with a sentence of reasoning. It takes a few minutes and repays them many times: when Coastline asks why online sales grow 12% in 2028, the answer is already in the model, and when an assumption turns out wrong, Ana can see which other numbers rested on the same thinking.

chapters.title: Contribution: what each new activity adds

scenes.head: For a new activity, the useful measure is its contribution: the revenue it brings in less the costs it causes, both variable and its own fixed costs…

segs.say: For a new activity, the useful measure is its contribution: the revenue it brings in less the costs it causes, both variable and its own fixed costs, before the business’s shared overheads. It answers “is the business better or worse off for doing this?” year by year.
Contribution of the two new activities (dollars)

scenes.head: Cold Brew loses $19,286 in 2028: its launch year carries $30,000 of promotion, the $6,000 launch and a full year of the brand manager against only…

segs.say: Cold Brew loses $19,286 in 2028: its launch year carries $30,000 of promotion, the $6,000 launch and a full year of the brand manager against only 30,000 cans. From 2029 it contributes $20,071 and more. The kitchen contributes from its first nine months, because its sales ramp up faster than its costs. This is why the total forecast has a dip in 2028, and the table shows exactly where it comes from.

chapters.title: The forecast to EBITDA, and what it says

scenes.head: The forecast to EBITDA, and what it says

segs.say: Lantern’s forecast income statement to EBITDA (dollars)

scenes.head: Read a forecast as a story, then test the story.

segs.say: Read a forecast as a story, then test the story. Revenue rises 48% in 2028, mostly from three new things (the kitchen, Cold Brew and a full year of cafés), then growth slows to 3.4% by 2032 as the new lines mature. Gross margin hardly moves (61.4% to 61.0%) because each line keeps its cost share. EBITDA margin falls to 2.7% in 2028, below the normalised 12.7% of 2027, then climbs to 13.0% by 2032 as fixed costs are spread over more sales. A lender reads that as a business taking a year of risk to grow, and will want module 2’s cash flow to show that 2028 can be financed.

scenes.head: Test the forecast against the world

segs.say: Test the forecast against the world. Every assumption should survive three questions. Has the history shown anything like it? (Online growth of 12% is slower than 2027’s, from a young business: plausible.) Does it imply something absurd? (By 2032 Cold Brew sells 60,000 cans; is there shelf space and demand for that?) Who would disagree, and why? Optimistic forecasts are the commonest cause of bad lending and investment decisions, which F05 called forecasting risk. Module 3 tests Lantern’s forecast with scenarios.

scenes.head: Revenue as price times volume

segs.say: Revenue as price times volume: Rₜ = Qₜ × Pₜ.
Rₜ: Revenue in year t ($).
Qₜ: Units sold in year t (workshop places, cans) (units).
Pₜ: Price per unit received by the business, net of any trade margin ($).
It assumes this: Volume and price are forecast separately; neither depends on the other unless the model says so.

scenes.head: Calendarising a project year that starts in month m

segs.say: Calendarising a project year that starts in month m: Cₜ = (13−m)/12 Pₜ + (m−1)/12 Pₜ₋₁.
Cₜ: The amount in calendar year t ($).
Pₜ: The amount in the project year that starts in calendar year t ($).
m: The month the project year starts (4 for April).
Pₜ₋₁: The amount in the project year before (zero before the start) ($).
It assumes this: Each project year’s amount falls evenly across its twelve months.

scenes.head: A fixed cost rising with inflation

segs.say: A fixed cost rising with inflation: Fₜ = F₀ (1 + i)ᵗ.
Fₜ: The fixed cost in forecast year t (t = 1 for 2028) ($).
F₀: The cost in the base year, on a full-year basis ($).
i: The assumed annual rate of increase (pay rises, price inflation).
It assumes this: No step changes; a new block of fixed costs is added as its own line.

scenes.head: Contribution of an activity

segs.say: Contribution of an activity: Contribution = Revenue − Variable costs − Its own fixed costs.
Its own fixed costs: Fixed costs that exist only because of the activity (its rent, its staff, its promotion) ($).
It assumes this: Shared overheads are excluded; they would be paid with or without the activity.

chapters.title: Example: Training revenue as price times volume

scenes.head: Training revenue as price times volume

segs.say: Ana plans 30 barista workshops in 2028, each for 12 participants at $130, rising to 36 workshops at $150 by 2032. In 2027 Lantern ran 24 workshops at $125. Forecast training revenue for 2028 and 2032, and compare 2028 with 2027.

scenes.head: Training revenue as price times volume

segs.say: Step 1. 2028: 30 workshops × 12 participants × $130 = 46,800 dollars.
Step 4. Split the growth: volume alone (30 instead of 24 workshops at $125) would give 45,000, so most of the rise is volume; the fee rise adds 1,800.

scenes.head: Training revenue as price times volume

segs.say: A growth rate of 30% for training would look aggressive on its own. Shown as six more workshops and a $5 higher fee, it can be judged: does Ana have the Saturdays, and will customers pay $130?

chapters.title: Example: The second kitchen in calendar years

scenes.head: The second kitchen in calendar years

segs.say: F05 forecast the kitchen’s revenue as $150,000, $185,000, $205,000, $215,000 and $220,000 in its project years, each running April to March from 1 April 2028; its fixed costs are $40,000 a year and its rent $30,000; variable costs are 42% of its sales. Find its revenue and contribution for calendar 2028 and 2029.

scenes.head: The second kitchen in calendar years

segs.say: Step 1. Months: calendar 2028 holds April–December of project year 1 (9 months). Calendar 2029 holds January–March of project year 1 (3 months) and April–December of project year 2 (9 months).
Step 3. Costs: variable 42% of revenue: 47,250 and 74,025. Fixed costs and rent are calendarised too: 2028 = 9/12 × (40,000 + 30,000) = 52,500; 2029 = 70,000.

scenes.head: The second kitchen in calendar years

segs.say: Revenue $112,500 and $176,250; contribution $12,750 and $32,225.

Calendarising matters most at the start and the end of a project. Treating project year 1 as calendar 2028 would have put $150,000 of kitchen revenue (and $70,000 of fixed costs) into a year in which the kitchen traded nine months.

chapters.title: Example: Why 2028 dips, and what Coastline will ask

scenes.head: Why 2028 dips, and what Coastline will ask

segs.say: The forecast shows EBITDA of $23,319 in 2028 (2.7% of revenue), against a normalised $73,587 in 2027, then $84,693 in 2029. Explain the dip to Coastline’s credit officer with figures from the model.

scenes.head: Why 2028 dips, and what Coastline will ask

segs.say: Step 1. Cold Brew’s launch: revenue 64,914, cost of goods 22,200, promotion, listing, brand manager and launch 62,000: a contribution of −19,286. In 2029, with promotion down to $18,000 and 45,000 cans, it is +20,071.
Step 2. The kitchen contributes 12,750 in its nine months of 2028, rising to 32,225 in 2029.
Step 3. Fixed wages rise to 185,194 with the cafés’ full year and 3% pay rises, and the cafés’ full-year leases add 8,000 to occupancy against 2027.
Step 4. Together these take EBITDA from the normalised 73,587 down to 23,319 in 2028; as Cold Brew turns positive and the kitchen ramps up, it reaches 84,693 in 2029 and 153,477 by 2032.

scenes.head: Why 2028 dips, and what Coastline will ask

segs.say: The 2028 dip is planned: Cold Brew’s launch costs (−$19,286 contribution) and a year of higher fixed costs, partly offset by the kitchen’s +$12,750.

A lender is not alarmed by a planned dip; it is alarmed by one nobody can explain. The question that follows is about cash, not profit: can Lantern pay its loan and keep its current ratio above 1.2 through 2028? Module 2 builds the cash flow to answer it.

scenes.head: Lantern’s forecast to EBITDA (fictional case; assumptions are Ana’s and F05’s)

segs.say: The whole forecast to EBITDA on one sheet. The inputs are rows 3–11 and column B; everything below row 26 is formulas. Try cutting online growth to 5% a year, or Cold Brew to 20,000 cans in 2028, and watch the EBITDA margin in row 45. Show formulas to see one formula per row. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Growing the wrong base

segs.say: Growing the wrong base. A base year that is a part year (Lantern’s cafés) or contains one-offs makes every later year wrong. Forecast from the normalised, twelve-month figure.

scenes.head: One growth rate for the whole business

segs.say: One growth rate for the whole business. Total revenue grown at one rate hides the fact that Lantern’s lines grow for different reasons and at different speeds, and makes it impossible to test any of them. Forecast each line from its own driver.

scenes.head: Treating fixed costs as a share of sales

segs.say: Treating fixed costs as a share of sales. Rent, salaries and leases do not rise with sales. Forecast them as amounts that grow with inflation or step up with capacity; use percent-of-sales only for small, mixed costs.

scenes.head: Forgetting to calendarise

segs.say: Forgetting to calendarise. A project forecast in its own years (April to March) dropped into calendar columns overstates the first year and misplaces every year after. Spread each project year over the calendar years it covers.

scenes.head: Growth without the step in costs

segs.say: Growth without the step in costs. Sales that grow past what the current kitchen, café or team can handle need new capacity. If the forecast grows sales but not the step costs that make the growth possible, it is too optimistic.

scenes.head: A smooth forecast with no story

segs.say: A smooth forecast with no story. If every line grows at a steady rate and every margin is flat, the forecast probably reflects arithmetic, not the business. A real plan has launches, ramp-ups and slowdowns; show them and explain them.

scenes.head: In a company, the revenue forecast is usually built bottom-up by the people closest to each line (store managers, the head of online, the sales team)…

segs.say: In a company, the revenue forecast is usually built bottom-up by the people closest to each line (store managers, the head of online, the sales team) and then challenged top-down by finance, which compares the total with the market’s growth and the company’s history. Where the two disagree, the gap is the most useful part of the exercise: it shows which assumptions someone is optimistic about.

scenes.head: Lenders and investors read the cost side as closely as the revenue side.

segs.say: Lenders and investors read the cost side as closely as the revenue side. A forecast whose margins rise every year needs a reason: fixed costs spread over growing sales, as in Lantern’s case, or a cheaper supplier, or a price rise. A credit committee will ask what happens to the margin if revenue grows half as fast, and a model whose fixed costs are genuinely fixed will show the margin falling, which is the honest answer.

scenes.head: Ana’s forecast to EBITDA is done: six revenue lines from their drivers, costs that behave as they do, and the second kitchen and Cold Brew…

segs.say: Ana’s forecast to EBITDA is done: six revenue lines from their drivers, costs that behave as they do, and the second kitchen and Cold Brew calendarised and visible. EBITDA dips to $23,319 in 2028 and recovers to $153,477 by 2032. Below EBITDA she still needs depreciation, interest and tax, and to know whether 2028’s cash is enough. Module 2 builds the schedules for working capital, capital spending and debt, and links the three statements.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Forecast each revenue line from the driver that explains it: growth on a sound base, price times volume, capacity, or market size and share.
Grow established lines from a normalised, twelve-month base; forecast new activities from their own plans.
Calendarise projects whose years do not match the model’s: each calendar year takes the months of each project year that fall in it.
Forecast variable costs as shares of the lines they serve, fixed costs as amounts rising with inflation, and step costs as new blocks when capacity runs out.
Use percent-of-sales only for small, mixed costs; it misstates fixed costs.
Contribution (revenue less variable and its own fixed costs) shows what each new activity adds, year by year.
Read the forecast as a story, explain every dip and rise, and test the assumptions against the history and the world.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
